```{r}
#| include: false
m_true <- glm(f_true, data = dev, family = binomial)
m_all <- glm(f_all, data = dev, family = binomial)
x_all <- model.matrix(f_all, dev)[, -1]; xv_all <- model.matrix(f_all, val)[, -1]
set.seed(1); cv_r <- cv.glmnet(x_all, dev$diabetes, family = "binomial", alpha = 0); cv_l <- cv.glmnet(x_all, dev$diabetes, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
val$risk <- predict(m_true, newdata = val, type = "response"); lpv <- qlogis(val$risk)
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Sessions 1 to 4: build, evaluate, internally validate, shrink
- Today: the **real test**: a **different district**, 2,000 adults, **never used for fitting**
- By the end you can:
  - **validate externally** (discrimination, calibration)
  - **recalibrate** a model for a new setting
  - judge **clinical usefulness** with a **decision curve**
  - **report** with TRIPOD
:::

# Topic 1 — Validation in a new district {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Discrimination and average calibration

```{r}
roc_v <- roc(val$diabetes, val$risk, quiet = TRUE)
c(auc = as.numeric(auc(roc_v)), predicted = mean(val$risk), observed = mean(val$diabetes)) |> round(3)
ci.auc(roc_v)
```

::: {.key}
**AUC 0.71** (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74): **lower** than the apparent 0.80 and the bootstrap-corrected 0.776. **Mean predicted risk 17.9%** vs **24.6% observed**: the model **under-estimates** risk in this district (older, less active, higher prevalence).
:::

## Calibration slope and plot

```{r}
c(slope = coef(glm(diabetes ~ lpv, data = val, family = binomial))[["lpv"]], intercept_offset = coef(glm(diabetes ~ offset(lpv), data = val, family = binomial))[[1]]) |> round(2)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4.4
calv <- val |> mutate(decile = ntile(risk, 10)) |> group_by(decile) |> summarise(predicted = mean(risk), observed = mean(diabetes))
ggplot(calv, aes(predicted, observed)) + geom_abline(linetype = 2) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = col_red) + geom_line(colour = col_red) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 0.7), ylim = c(0, 0.7)) + labs(x = "Mean predicted risk", y = "Observed proportion with diabetes")
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Slope 0.67**: predictions are **too extreme** (low risks too low, high risks too high): some **overfitting** and **weaker effects** in the new district
- **Intercept +0.50** (calibration-in-the-large): risk **under-estimated on average**
- Typical of **external validation**: performance **drops** and **calibration** needs updating
:::

## Which development strategy transports best?

```{r}
slope_of <- function(lp) coef(glm(diabetes ~ lp, data = val, family = binomial))[["lp"]]
lps <- list(ML_8 = predict(m_true, val), ML_all = predict(m_all, val), ridge = as.numeric(predict(cv_r, xv_all, s = "lambda.min")), lasso = as.numeric(predict(cv_l, xv_all, s = "lambda.1se")))
sapply(lps, function(lp) c(auc = auc_of(val$diabetes, lp), slope = slope_of(lp))) |> t() |> round(2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- The **all-markers** ML model is the **worst calibrated** (slope **0.53**) and has the lowest AUC (0.69)
- **Ridge**: slope **0.80**, closest to 1 among the full models
- **Lasso at λ.1se**: slope **1.59**: **over-shrunk** (too narrow)
- **No strategy fully repairs** the change of population: that needs **recalibration**
:::

# Topic 2 — Updating and usefulness {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Recalibration

```{r}
rec <- glm(diabetes ~ lpv, data = val, family = binomial)
val$risk_rec <- predict(rec, type = "response")
c(brier_before = mean((val$risk - val$diabetes)^2), brier_after = mean((val$risk_rec - val$diabetes)^2)) |> round(3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Recalibrate**: re-estimate the **intercept** (and the **slope**) in the new setting; keep the predictors and relative weights
- **Brier 0.170 to 0.165**; the **AUC does not change** (only the calibration)
- Better than **refitting everything** on a small local sample (overfitting), but needs **local outcome data**
- Models need **updating over time** and across **settings**
:::

## Decision curve: net benefit

::: {.eq}
net benefit = TP / n − FP / n × t / (1 − t)       t = the risk threshold at which you would act
:::

```{r}
nb <- function(risk, y, t) { tp <- sum(risk >= t & y == 1); fp <- sum(risk >= t & y == 0); tp / length(y) - fp / length(y) * t / (1 - t) }
ts <- seq(0.05, 0.40, 0.05)
tibble(threshold = ts, model = sapply(ts, \(t) nb(val$risk_rec, val$diabetes, t)), treat_all = sapply(ts, \(t) mean(val$diabetes) - (1 - mean(val$diabetes)) * t / (1 - t))) |> mutate(across(-threshold, \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Reading the decision curve

::: {.key}
**Treat none = 0.** The model has the **same** net benefit as **treat-all** up to a threshold of **10%**, and a **clearly higher** one from **15%** (0.126 vs 0.112) up to 40%, where treating everyone becomes **harmful** (negative above about 25%). A net benefit of **0.10 at 20%** is like finding **10 extra true cases per 100 adults with no unnecessary test**. **Choose the threshold from costs and benefits**, not from the AUC.
:::

## Reporting: TRIPOD

::: {.good}
- **Source of data**, setting, **outcome**, **predictors** and their measurement
- **Sample size** and **events**; handling of **missing data**
- The **full model** (**intercept and all coefficients**) so others can use it
- **Performance**: AUC, **calibration** (plot, slope, intercept), with CIs
- **Internal validation** (bootstrap) and **external validation**, any **updating**
- **Limitations** and intended **use** (threshold, who)
:::

::: {.key}
*Example:* "The model (logistic regression, 8 predictors, 84 events in 700 adults) had an apparent AUC of 0.80 (bootstrap-corrected 0.78); in an external cohort of 2,000 adults the AUC was 0.71, the calibration slope 0.67 and risk was under-estimated (mean 17.9% vs 24.6% observed)."
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p5q1", "The AUC is 0.80 in development and 0.71 in the external cohort. What is the most likely reason?",
         c("The external cohort is larger, and large cohorts give lower AUCs",
           "The model was fitted to the external cohort and is therefore too optimistic",
           "AUC values cannot be compared between cohorts",
           "A different case-mix and weaker predictor effects, plus some overfitting"), answer = 4,
         explain = "External validation usually shows lower performance because of overfitting and because the new population has a different case-mix or different predictor effects.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p5q2", "The mean predicted risk is 17.9% and the observed risk 24.6% in the external cohort. What does this show?",
         c("Poor calibration-in-the-large: risk is under-estimated in this district",
           "Poor discrimination: the model cannot rank the adults correctly",
           "Good calibration, because both numbers are in the same range",
           "Overfitting in the development data, which the calibration slope measures"), answer = 1,
         explain = "A mean predicted risk below the observed prevalence means the model under-estimates risk on average. This is a different problem from poor ranking or too-extreme predictions.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p5q3", "What does an external calibration slope of 0.67 mean?",
         c("Risks are under-estimated by 33% for all of the patients in the cohort",
           "Predictions are too extreme: low risks too low, high risks too high",
           "The model gets two thirds of the patients right in the new cohort",
           "The AUC is 0.67 in the validation cohort and 0.80 in development"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A slope below 1 shows that the predicted risks vary more than the true risks. Shrinking the linear predictor by the slope would fix this.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p5q4", "What is a decision curve used for?",
         c("To plot the ROC curves of several different cohorts together on one graph",
           "To find the risk threshold that gives the highest AUC for the model",
           "To compare the calibration slopes of competing models in one picture",
           "To show the net benefit of the model at different risk thresholds"), answer = 4,
         explain = "A decision curve weighs true positives against false positives at the threshold where a clinician would act, and compares the model with treating everybody or nobody.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p5q5", "Which item is essential in a report of a model that others will want to use?",
         c("The full equation with the intercept, and how it was validated",
           "The p-value of each predictor in the final model, with its estimate",
           "The software code that was used to draw the ROC curve in the paper",
           "The name of the statistician who developed the model and their institute"), answer = 1,
         explain = "TRIPOD asks for the complete model so that risks can be calculated by others, together with its performance and validation.")
```
